parts.problem_md:
Acyl chlorides, amino acids, and polyamides are important nitrogen-containing organic compounds.

Ethanoyl chloride, CH<sub>3</sub>COCl, reacts vigorously with ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub>, to form an amide.

i) State the name of the mechanism of this reaction.

[1]

ii) Draw the mechanism for this reaction. Include all relevant curly arrows, lone pairs, and dipoles.

[4]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The name of the mechanism is:
> 
> - Addition-elimination / nucleophilic addition-elimination **[1 mark]**

ii) The mechanism for the reaction of ethanoyl chloride with ammonia is:

![Mechanism step 1: ethanoyl chloride with δ+ on carbonyl carbon and δ- on oxygen; curly arrow from lone pair on N in NH3 pointing to the carbonyl carbon](assets/001-mechanism-step-1-ethanoyl-chloride-with-on-carbo.png)

![Mechanism step 2: tetrahedral intermediate formed with O^-^ charge on oxygen and N^+^ charge on nitrogen clearly shown](assets/002-mechanism-step-2-tetrahedral-intermediate-formed.png)

(Deprotonation of nitrogen — not required for full credit)

![Mechanism step 3: curly arrows showing O^-^ lone pair reforming C=O double bond and C–Cl bond breaking to release Cl^-^, giving ethanamide product](assets/003-mechanism-step-3-curly-arrows-showing-o-lone-pai.png)

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Dipole on C=O bond with δ<sup>+</sup> on C and δ<sup>-</sup> on O **[1 mark]**
> - Curly arrow from lone pair on N of NH<sub>3</sub> to carbonyl carbon
> **AND**
> Curly arrow showing C=O π bond breaking to O<sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - Correct tetrahedral intermediate with O<sup>-</sup> and N<sup>+</sup> charges **[1 mark]**
> - Curly arrow from lone pair on O<sup>-</sup> to reform C=O
> **AND**
> Curly arrow breaking C–Cl bond to Cl<sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> Allow deprotonation of nitrogen in a subsequent step

> **[exam-tip]**
> In acyl chloride mechanisms, most marks are lost on arrow starts/ends and charges. Make sure your first arrow starts from the lone pair on N in NH<sub>3</sub> and points to the carbonyl carbon, and your second arrow moves the C=O π bond onto oxygen to give O<sup>-</sup>.
> 
> In the intermediate, check you have both O<sup>-</sup> and N<sup>+</sup> shown. When the carbonyl reforms, you need two arrows simultaneously: O<sup>-</sup> back to C=O and C–Cl breaking to Cl<sup>-</sup>.

parts.problem_md:
1,6-diaminohexane reacts with hexanedioic acid to form a polyamide called Nylon 6,6.

i) Draw the structure of the repeat unit of Nylon 6,6.

[2]

ii) Polyesters and polyamides are biodegradable polymers, whereas polyalkenes are generally non-biodegradable.

Explain this difference in terms of the structure and reactivity of the polymer chains.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
i) The structure of the repeat unit of Nylon 6,6 is:

![Chemical structure of the Nylon 6,6 repeat unit showing the amide linkage –NH–CO– connecting a hexamethylene diamine chain and an adipoyl chain](assets/005-chemical-structure-of-the-nylon-6-6-repeat-unit-.png)

Structure of repeat unit: −NH(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>6</sub>NH−CO(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>4</sub>CO−

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Correct amide linkage shown, i.e. –NH–CO– **[1 mark]**
> - Correct carbon backbone on both sides of the amide link, i.e. –NH(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>6</sub>NH– and –CO(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>4</sub>CO– **[1 mark]**
> 
> Acceptable representation includes, for example:
> −NH(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>6</sub>NH−CO(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>4</sub>CO−

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) Polyesters and polyamides are biodegradable polymers, whereas polyalkenes are generally non-biodegradable because:
> 
> - Polyesters / polyamides contain polar ester / amide linkages which can be hydrolysed (by acids, alkalis, or bacteria) **[1 mark]**
> - Polyalkenes contain non-polar C–C bonds and C–H bonds which are chemically unreactive and cannot be hydrolysed **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When explaining biodegradability, focus on bond type and reactivity rather than just stating the compound breaks down. Polar ester and amide bonds are susceptible to hydrolysis because water molecules can attack the δ<sup>+</sup> carbonyl carbon. Non-polar C–C and C–H bonds in polyalkenes have no such dipole and do not react with water.

parts.problem_md:
State the relative order of acidity of benzoic acid, phenylmethanol and 4-methylphenol shown in Fig. 1.1, starting with the most acidic. Explain your reasoning.

![Structural formulae of three organic compounds: benzoic acid (C₆H₅COOH), phenylmethanol (C₆H₅CH₂OH), and 4-methylphenol (4-CH₃-C₆H₄-OH)](assets/006-structural-formulae-of-three-organic-compounds-b.jpeg)

**Fig. 1.1**
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The relative order of acidity and reasoning are:
> 
> - Benzoic acid > 4-methylphenol > phenylmethanol **[1 mark]**
> - The benzoate ion is stabilised by delocalisation of negative charge over two electronegative oxygen atoms 
> **OR**
> The C=O group withdraws electron density from the O–H bond **[1 mark]**
> - The 4-methylphenoxide ion is stabilised by delocalisation of the oxygen lone pair into the benzene ring **[1 mark]**
> - The alkoxide ion of phenylmethanol is destabilised by the electron-donating CH<sub>2</sub> group 
> **OR**
> The alkyl group donates electron density to the oxygen, making it less stable **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The relative acidity depends on the stability of the conjugate base (the anion formed after losing H<sup>+</sup>). The more stable the anion, the more readily the compound donates a proton.
> 
> The benzoate ion is particularly stable because the negative charge is delocalised over two electronegative oxygen atoms. The phenoxide ion is less stable as the charge is delocalised into carbon atoms in the ring. The alkoxide ion from phenylmethanol is destabilised by the electron-donating effect of the benzyl group.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

State the relative order of acidity of benzoic acid, phenylmethanol and 4-methylphenol shown in Fig. 1.1, starting with the most acidic. Explain your reasoning.

Fig. 1.1 shows structural formulae of three organic compounds: benzoic acid (C₆H₅COOH), phenylmethanol (C₆H₅CH₂OH), and 4-methylphenol (4-CH₃-C₆H₄-OH)

The ester 4-methylphenyl benzoate can be formed in **two** steps from two of the compounds shown in Fig. 1.1 in part **(a)**.

i) Draw the **skeletal** formula of 4-methylphenyl benzoate.

[1]

ii) State the **two**-step route for the synthesis of 4-methylphenyl benzoate. Include reagents and conditions for each step and the structure of the intermediate compound.

[5]
parts.solution_md:
i) The skeletal formula of 4-methylphenyl benzoate is:

![Skeletal formula of 4-methylphenyl benzoate showing a benzoyl group esterified with a 4-methylphenol ring](assets/007-skeletal-formula-of-4-methylphenyl-benzoate-show.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) A two-step route for the synthesis of 4-methylphenyl benzoate:
> 
> - Starting materials: 4-methylphenol
> **AND**
> Benzoic acid **[1 mark]**
> - Step 1: react benzoic acid with SOCl<sub>2</sub> / PCl<sub>5</sub> / PCl<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - Intermediate: benzoyl chloride / C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COCl **[1 mark]**
> - Step 2: react benzoyl chloride with 4-methylphenol dissolved in NaOH(aq) / sodium hydroxide solution **[1 mark]**
> - Step 2 condition: at room temperature / shake with the acyl chloride **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Phenols do not react directly with carboxylic acids to form esters, so the carboxylic acid must first be converted to the more reactive acyl chloride using SOCl<sub>2</sub>, PCl<sub>5</sub>, or PCl<sub>3</sub>.
> 
> In step 2, NaOH(aq) is required to form the phenoxide ion, which acts as the nucleophile in the addition-elimination reaction with the acyl chloride. Without the base, the phenol reacts too slowly.

parts.problem_md: State the reagents and conditions required to form benzoic acid from methylbenzene.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reagents and conditions required to form benzoic acid from methylbenzene are:
> 
> - Alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub> / potassium manganate(VII) **[1 mark]**
> - Dilute acid / dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> / dilute HCl **[1 mark]**
> - Heat
> **AND**
> Reflux **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The reaction involves two stages: alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub> under reflux oxidises the methyl side chain to give potassium benzoate, which is then acidified with dilute acid to release benzoic acid. Reagents and conditions for both stages must be stated to gain full marks.

parts.problem_md:
The acyl chloride, ethanedioyl dichloride is shown in Fig. 3.1.

This can be synthesised from compound **X** in a single step.

![Structural formula of ethanedioyl dichloride (ClCOCOCl) showing two acyl chloride groups connected by a C–C bond](assets/008-structural-formula-of-ethanedioyl-dichloride-clc.png)

**Fig. 3.1**

Deduce the identity of compound **X**.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The identity of compound X is:
> 
> - HO<sub>2</sub>C–CO<sub>2</sub>H (ethanedioic acid)
> **OR**
> HO<sub>2</sub>C–COCl **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Ethanedioyl dichloride has two acyl chloride groups (–COCl). To form it in a single step, compound X must have at least one group that can be converted to –COCl. If X is the dicarboxylic acid (ethanedioic acid, HO<sub>2</sub>C–CO<sub>2</sub>H), both –OH groups are replaced by –Cl in one reaction. If X already has one –COCl group, it is the half-converted intermediate.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

The acyl chloride, ethanedioyl dichloride is shown in Fig. 3.1.

This can be synthesised from compound **X** in a single step.

The identity of compound X is:

- HO₂C–CO₂H (ethanedioic acid)

OR

HO₂C–COCl

State the reagents and conditions needed to convert **X i**nto ClCOCOCl.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A suitable reagent to convert compound X into ethanedioyl dichloride is:
> 
> - SOCl<sub>2</sub>
> **OR**
> PCl<sub>5</sub>
> **OR**
> PCl<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> SOCl<sub>2</sub>, PCl<sub>5</sub>, and PCl<sub>3</sub> all convert the –OH group of a carboxylic acid to –Cl to form an acyl chloride. PCl<sub>3</sub> requires heating to drive the reaction; SOCl<sub>2</sub> and PCl<sub>5</sub> react readily at room temperature.

parts.problem_md:
A different acyl chloride was used to synthesise ethyl butanoate.

i) Draw the displayed formula of the acyl chloride.

[1]

ii) State the name of the mechanism by which ethyl butanoate is formed.

[1]

iii) State the name of the other product formed in this reaction.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
i) The displayed formula of the acyl chloride used to synthesise ethyl butanoate is:

![Displayed formula of butanoyl chloride showing all bonds including C–H bonds along the four-carbon chain, the C=O bond, and the C–Cl bond](assets/009-displayed-formula-of-butanoyl-chloride-showing-a.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct displayed formula

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The name of the mechanism by which ethyl butanoate is formed is:
> 
> - Nucleophilic addition-elimination **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The other product formed in this reaction is:
> 
> - HCl / hydrogen chloride **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In the name ethyl butanoate, the ‘ethyl’ part comes from the alcohol used (ethanol) and the ‘butanoate’ part comes from the acyl chloride (butanoyl chloride). The other product of any reaction between an acyl chloride and an alcohol is always HCl.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Benzoic acid can be formed from the oxidation of methylbenzene.

i) State the reagents and conditions needed to oxidise methylbenzene to benzoic acid.

[3]

ii) State **two** observations that could be made during this reaction.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The reagents and conditions needed to oxidise methylbenzene to benzoic acid are:
> 
> - Alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub> / potassium manganate(VII) **[1 mark]**
> - Dilute acid / dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> / dilute HCl **[1 mark]**
> - Heat
> **AND**
> Reflux **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Two observations that could be made during this reaction are:
> 
> - Solution loses purple colour **[1 mark]**
> - Brown precipitate (of MnO<sub>2</sub>) forms **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The oxidation of methylbenzene is a two-stage process: the side chain is first oxidised under alkaline conditions to give potassium benzoate, then acidification with dilute acid releases benzoic acid. Both the alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub> and the dilute acid must be stated.
> 
> Unlike the oxidation of primary alcohols (where acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub> gives a colourless solution as Mn<sup>7+</sup> is reduced to Mn<sup>2+</sup>), the oxidation of methylbenzene under alkaline conditions produces a brown precipitate of MnO<sub>2</sub> because Mn<sup>7+</sup> is only reduced to Mn<sup>4+</sup>.

parts.problem_md: Construct an equation to show that benzoic acid acts as a weak acid.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COOH (aq) ⇌ C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COO<sup>-</sup> (aq) + H<sup>+</sup> (aq) **[1 mark]**
> 
> The reversible sign (⇌) must be present
> 
> State symbols are not required

> **[exam-tip]**
> Benzoic acid is a weak acid and only partially dissociates in aqueous solution, so the equilibrium position lies to the left. Do not use a one-way arrow as this would imply complete dissociation, which is incorrect for a weak acid.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Benzoic acid can be formed from methylbenzene. 

This process occurs in two stages. 

methylbenzene       \$\$\overset{Step 1}{\rightarrow}\$\$   potassium benzoate    \$\$\overset{Step 2}{\rightarrow}\$\$  benzoic acid

i) State the type of reaction that takes place in **step 1**.

[1]

ii) State the reagents and conditions needed for **step 1** and **step 2** of this reaction.

[3]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The type of reaction taking place in step 1 is:
> 
> - Oxidation **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The reagents and conditions needed for step 1 and step 2 are:
> 
> - Step 1: Alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub> / potassium manganate(VII) **[1 mark]**
> - Step 1 condition: Heat
> **AND**
> Reflux **[1 mark]**
> - Step 2: Dilute acid / dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> / dilute HCl **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Step 1 is the oxidation of the methyl side chain under alkaline conditions, which forms potassium benzoate. Step 2 is the acidification with dilute acid to protonate the carboxylate and release benzoic acid. Reagents and conditions for both steps must be stated.
> 
> Note that a specific acid such as dilute HCl or dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is accepted for step 2.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Benzoic acid can be formed from methylbenzene. 

This process occurs in two stages. 

methylbenzene → potassium benzoate → benzoic acid

i) The type of reaction taking place in step 1 is:
- Oxidation

ii) The reagents and conditions needed for step 1 and step 2 are:
- Step 1: Alkaline KMnO4 / potassium manganate(VII)
- Step 1 condition: Heat AND Reflux
- Step 2: Dilute acid / dilute H2SO4 / dilute HCl

State two observations that could be made during **step 1**.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Two observations that could be made during step 1 are:
> 
> - Solution changes from purple to colourless **[1 mark]**
> - Brown precipitate (of MnO<sub>2</sub>) forms **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The KMnO<sub>4</sub> solution is purple due to MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> ions (Mn<sup>7+</sup>). During the alkaline oxidation of methylbenzene, Mn<sup>7+</sup> is reduced to Mn<sup>4+</sup>, producing brown MnO<sub>2</sub> as a precipitate. The solution itself loses its purple colour as the MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> ions are consumed.

parts.problem_md: State the relative acidities of benzoic acid and phenol. Explain your reasoning.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The relative acidities of benzoic acid and phenol are:
> 
> - Benzoic acid is a stronger acid than phenol **[1 mark]**
> - The C=O group in benzoic acid withdraws electron density from the O–H bond (negative inductive effect) **[1 mark]**
> - This weakens the O–H bond, making it easier to release H<sup>+</sup> / the proton **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The stronger an acid, the more easily it donates a proton (H<sup>+</sup>). In benzoic acid, the adjacent C=O group withdraws electron density from the O–H bond, stabilising the benzoate anion and making proton release easier.
> 
> In phenol, the oxygen lone pair is donated into the benzene ring, which reduces the electron density available on the oxygen. However, phenol has no carbonyl group to further weaken the O–H bond, so it is a weaker acid than benzoic acid (though stronger than aliphatic alcohols).

parts.problem_md:
Fig. 2.1 shows three different molecules.

![Structural formulae of propan-1-ol, propanoic acid, and phenol](assets/013-structural-formulae-of-propan-1-ol-propanoic-aci.png)

**Fig. 2.1**

Propan-1-ol can react with sodium metal.

Construct an equation for this reaction.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for the reaction of propan-1-ol with sodium is:
> 
> - 2C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>OH + 2Na → 2C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>ONa + H<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When an alcohol reacts with sodium, the O–H bond breaks and a sodium alkoxide salt and hydrogen gas are formed. The same reaction occurs with phenols and carboxylic acids, which are also more acidic than water.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Fig. 2.1 shows three different molecules.

Structural formulae of propan-1-ol, propanoic acid, and phenol

Fig. 2.1

i) State the relative order of acidity of propanoic acid, propan-1-ol and phenol, starting with the least acidic.

[1]

ii) Explain your answer to part **(b)(i)**.

[3]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The relative order of acidity, starting with the least acidic, is:
> 
> - Propan-1-ol, phenol, propanoic acid **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The explanation:
> 
> - In propanoic acid, the C=O group withdraws electron density from the O–H bond 
> **OR**
> The propanoate ion is stabilised by delocalisation of negative charge over two electronegative oxygen atoms **[1 mark]**
> - In phenol, the O–H bond is weakened by the negative inductive effect of the benzene ring 
> **OR**
> The phenoxide ion is stabilised by delocalisation of the oxygen lone pair into the ring **[1 mark]**
> - In propan-1-ol, the O–H bond is strengthened by the positive inductive effect of the alkyl group 
> **OR**
> The propoxide ion is destabilised by the electron-donating alkyl group **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When explaining relative acidity, always refer to the stability of the conjugate base (the anion formed after losing H<sup>+</sup>). The more stable the anion, the more readily the compound donates a proton. Propanoic acid forms the most stable anion because the negative charge is delocalised over two electronegative oxygen atoms.

parts.problem_md:
Methanoic acid and propanoic acid can be distinguished by a simple chemical test.

i) State the name of a reagent that could be used for this test.

[1]

ii) State which of these two acids gives a positive result with your chosen reagent, and state the observation you would make.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) A reagent that could be used for this test is:
> 
> Any **one **from:
> 
> - Tollens' reagent
> - Fehling's solution
> - Acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub>
> - Acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>
> 
> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii)
> 
> Any **one **from:
> 
> - Methanoic acid gives a positive result with Tollens' reagent **AND** silver mirror forms
> - Methanoic acid gives a positive result with Fehling's solution **AND** red / orange precipitate forms
> - Methanoic acid gives a positive result with acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub> **AND** solution turns colourless
> - Methanoic acid gives a positive result with acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> **AND** solution turns green
> 
> **[1 mark]**
> 
> The observation stated must be consistent with the reagent chosen in part (i)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Methanoic acid is unusual among carboxylic acids because it contains a CHO-type group. The hydrogen atom directly bonded to the carbonyl carbon can act as a reducing agent. This means methanoic acid, unlike propanoic acid, gives a positive result with oxidising agents such as Tollens' reagent and Fehling's solution.
> 
> Make sure the observation you describe is consistent with the reagent you named in part (i) as a mismatched reagent/observation pair will not gain the mark.
